newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus, gripped by political crisis, goes to polls.
newsitem.headline: Belarus, gripped by political crisis, goes to polls.

text.p: Belarussians on Sunday were completing voting in a controversial referendum in which hardline President Alexander Lukashenko is seeking to widen his powers over rival institutions and extend his term beyond 2000.

Polling stations opened at 6 a.m. (0400 GMT) and were due to close at 10 p.m. (2000 GMT) on the last day of a long process that began on November 9. Preliminary results should be available at some point on Monday, officials say.

The former Soviet republic was plunged back into political crisis on Saturday when Lukashnko and a rebellious parliament both reneged on a deal brokered by neighbouring Russia aimed at resolving their dispute over the referendum.

A defiant Lukashenko addressed the nation of 10 million people on state television on Saturday, pointing to religious and ethnic conflicts in other former Soviet republics and saying the country he runs is an island of stability.
The president wants to use the vote to tighten his grip on rival institutions, including parliament, and extend his term by more than two years -- an idea which parliamentarians oppose.

"It is not a choice between president and parliament. It is a choice between chaos and anarchy on one hand, and discipline, order and a changes for the better on the other," he said in the address, which was also broadcast simultaneously on two other channels used by Russian television in Belarus.

He declared only his draft constitution would bring stability, saying: "Look at the situation in the other former Soviet republics, the religious and ethnic conflicts. Only our country is an island of stability in this chaos and anarchy."

Communists, liberals and nationalists have recently joined forces to oppose Lukashenko, 42, and his authoritarian style of rule. But there is a lack of strong opposition leadership in the nation sandwiched between Russia and Poland.
The referendum poses seven questions, including one on whether to accept Lukashenko's draft constitution which would broaden his powers.

After a brief period on Friday when the compromise looked like holding, both Lukashenko and parliament reneged on the Russian-brokered deal the following day. Lukashenko compared deputies to animals in a zoo and said he had cancelled his half of the accord after the parliament failed to approve it.
Moscow is Lukashenko's closest ally and the Kremlin is seen as the only power with enough clout to influence him.
Russia's ORT television, which tends to back the Kremlin, broadcast an anti-Lukashenko item late on Saturday and a long interview with his main foe, parliament chief Semyon Sharetsky.
Lukashenko's voice was heard praising Adolf Hitler for bringing order to pre-World War Two Germany with footage of a concentration camp.
The foreign ministry sent a note of protest to the Russian ministry over the item on the "Vremya" analytical programme, saying Lukashenko's voice had been faked, the television said.
The row over the vote has many parallels with a stand-off in Moscow in 1993 between President Boris Yeltsin and deputies which Yeltsin ended by sending tanks against parliament.

The president said on Saturday he had decreed that Sunday's vote would be mandatory, contradicting the deal signed at dawn on Friday after personal mediation by Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.

Sharetsky, who signed the agreement, said: "The situation in Belarus is getting worse and tensions are growing. We thought we would be able to calm the storm. But the president wanted and still wants to grab more power by anti-constitutional means."

The constitutional court in Minsk put off until Tuesday a decision on a bid by deputies to remove Lukashenko from office by impeachment. A deputy who attended the court session said earlier that one judge was absent and the court was split 5-5.
